title: The journey of a library book
intro: You will hear part of a radio programme. A librarian, Mr Rahman, explains what happens to a library book after it is returned. Complete the flow chart and the fact box for questions 1 to 9. Write one or two words or a number for each answer. You will hear the recording twice.

script.text: Most people think that when you drop a book into the returns chute, a librarian picks it up and walks it back to the shelf. Twenty years ago that was true. Today the book goes on quite a journey, and almost nobody sees it.

First, the book slides down the chute onto a moving belt. Every one of our books has a small tag inside the back cover. As the book passes under a reader, the tag is scanned, and in less than a second the book is removed from your account. That is why your phone can show the book as returned before you have even left the building.

Second, the machine checks whether someone else is waiting for the book. If the book has been reserved, the belt pushes it into a red bin, and a member of staff sends it to the right branch that same evening.

If nobody is waiting, the book moves to the third stage, which is sorting. The machine reads the tag again and sends the book into one of twelve bins. There is a bin for children's picture books, a bin for cookery, a bin for Chinese fiction, and so on.

Fourth, each full bin is wheeled to its section by a robot trolley. The trolley follows a line of magnets under the carpet, so it never gets lost, although it does stop politely if a toddler stands in front of it.
Only the last stage still needs a person. A shelver takes the books from the bin and puts each one back in its exact place. We have tried machines for this, but human hands are still faster.

The whole journey takes about forty minutes. Our main branch handles roughly nine thousand books a day this way. And the most common thing we find left inside a returned book? Not money, sadly. It is receipts, usually from the supermarket.
